    A little human error

    Sometimes the barista loses count. Sometimes the customer orders the wrong thing.

    “Please redo it.”“Eh, I’ll take it.”

    “Nolal” means “eh, I’ll take it.” This sets the chance a customer accepts a mix-up. Everyone else asks for one remake. Faster isn’t always the drink they wanted.

    SOMETHING TO NOTICE

    A little breathing room goes a long way.

    When every barista is busy, even a small cluster of arrivals can create a long line. Try adding one person and replaying the same customers.

    FOLLOW YOUR CURIOSITY

    Four little experiments.

    No high scores. Just “oh, that’s why.”

    A TOY MODEL. A REAL IDEA.

    People aren’t averages.
    Neither are their waits.

    This café is a small experiment in queues, not a staffing forecast. Everyone wants one drink; some orders need a remake. Baristas work at the same speed. We leave out payment, walking, breaks, and a hundred other real-life details.

    What’s happening under the counter?

    The café accepts arrivals for 20 minutes, then finishes serving those who remain. Evenly spaced arrivals have fixed gaps; unpredictable arrivals use random exponential gaps with the same expected rate. Varied drinks take either 40% or 160% of the mean, with equal probability.

    Shared queues are first-come, first-served. For separate lines, each arrival joins a shortest line (including the person being served); ties rotate and nobody switches. Patience applies only before service. At the exact deadline, an available barista takes priority over leaving.

    Replay uses a fixed random seed. Customers keep their own arrival and drink times when staffing or queue policy changes. The 90th-percentile wait is the nearest-rank value: 90% of served customers waited that long or less. One run is an experiment, not a universal conclusion.

    Mix-ups and willingness to accept them use separate seeded draws. Half the mix-ups are ordering flusters, half barista slips. These are invented probabilities, not research measurements. At handover a customer either keeps the drink or asks for one guaranteed-correct remake on the same barista, taking the original drink time again. They do not rejoin the queue or abandon during service. Drink names in stories are illustrative, not a separate menu simulation. The three guided queue experiments switch mix-ups off.

    Everything runs in your browser. There are no model calls, trackers, or uploaded results. Run history lasts for this page visit.
